Null models of the trait-gradient analysis

Source: R/trait_gradient.R
trait_gradient_test.Rd

Compares the values of trait_gradient() with those of null communities. The default null ("species") keeps every community as observed and exchanges the trait means of species among species, so it asks whether the traits of species follow the sites they share. The curveball null ("curveball", Strona et al. 2014) keeps the traits and moves species among sites, with the richness of each site and the number of sites of each species fixed, so it asks whether the observed co-occurrences matter given the traits.

Usage

trait_gradient_test(
  x,
  n_null = 999,
  null = c("species", "phylo", "bm", "curveball", "permute"),
  burn_in = NULL,
  thin = NULL,
  tree = NULL,
  phylo_k = 1.1
)

Arguments

x

Result of trait_gradient().

n_null

Number of null communities.

null

"species" (the default), "phylo", "bm", "curveball" or "permute".

burn_in, thin

Trades of the curveball chain before the first null community and between null communities; by default 50 and 5 times the number of sites, so that each site takes part in about 10 trades between null communities.

tree

Phylogeny (phylo) with branch lengths, for null = "phylo" and "bm"; every species of x must be a tip.

phylo_k

The constant \(k \ge 1\) of the phylogenetic permutations of null = "phylo": closer to 1, more exchanges among relatives only.

Value

An object of class mc_trait_gradient_test, a list with statistics (one row per statistic: observed, null_mean, null_sd, ses and p), species (one row per species: observed \(\beta\) with ses_beta and p_beta, and with null = "species", "phylo" or "bm" also \(\alpha\) with ses_alpha and p_alpha), null (a matrix with one row per null community and one column per statistic) and the settings.

Details

Statistics: the correlation of \(\beta\) and \(\alpha\), the variance of \(\beta\) (how far species spread along the gradient) and the variance of \(\alpha\), and the \(\beta\) of each species. Tests are two-sided.

null = "species". The trait values of species \(i\) become \(t_{ij} - \bar t_i + \bar t_{\pi(i)}\) for a random permutation \(\pi\) of species: each species carries the mean of another and keeps its own variation among sites. Sites, abundances and co-occurrences stay as observed. This is the null for the variances: a large variance of \(\beta\) means that species with similar traits live in similar communities.

null = "curveball". Populations move among sites with their trait values and abundances by curveball trades; the chain starts at the observed communities and runs burn_in trades and then thin trades between null communities. Because it also breaks the turnover of species along the gradient, the variances of \(\beta\) and \(\alpha\) differ from the null whenever composition changes among sites, even when traits are unrelated to it: species that share sites share their site means. Use the curveball for the correlation only.

null = "permute", the null of Ackerly & Cornwell (2007), permutes the site of each population. It keeps the number of populations of each site but can place a species twice in one site, and it breaks the turnover of species as the curveball does.

null = "phylo". The phylogenetic permutations of Lapointe & Garland (2001): as "species", but the mean of a species moves preferably to a close relative. Patristic distances are scaled by the largest, \(d^*_{ij} = d_{ij} / d_{max}\), turned into similarities \(s_{ij} = k - d^*_{ij}\) with \(k\) = phylo_k \(\ge 1\), and each row is divided by its sum to give the probability \(p_{ij}\) that the mean of species \(i\) moves to species \(j\) (staying is the most likely move). Species are taken in random order, and each mean moves to a species not yet occupied, with the probabilities of the remaining species rescaled to sum to one; the last mean takes the last free species. Large \(k\) approaches "species" (equally likely permutations); on an ultrametric tree \(k = 1\) gives no exchange across the root. Lapointe & Garland (2001) illustrate \(k\) from 1.0 to 2. A species with no close relative keeps its own mean in many nulls (about half of them in our trials with \(k = 1.1\)), so the test has little power for such species.

null = "bm". The species means are replaced by values simulated by Brownian motion on tree, with the mean and rate estimated from the observed means by restricted maximum likelihood; each species keeps its own variation among sites. The null is a trait that evolves along the tree and has nothing to do with assembly.

Use "phylo" when the niches of species are conserved: under "species", a trait that merely shares the phylogenetic structure of the niches looks sorted along the gradient. "bm" is exact only when the trait does evolve by Brownian motion: a trait with less phylogenetic structure than Brownian motion makes its variance tests reject (see Validation).

The \(\alpha\) of a species is not tested under "curveball" and "permute": the species mean does not change, so its test would mirror that of \(\beta\).

Validation

In simulated metacommunities (25 species, 20 sites, 150 replicates per scenario, 5% level, leave-one-out site means) with trait means drawn independently of the niches, the species null rejected in 4.7% (variance of \(\beta\)), 5.3% (variance of \(\alpha\)) and 7.3% (correlation) of replicates; the curveball rejected in 5.3% for the correlation but in 26–66% for the variances. With traits that sort species along the gradient, all tests rejected in 98–100%. When the trait and the niches both evolve along the tree, the species null rejected in 10–17% although the trait plays no part in assembly: related species share both sites and trait values, and the test detects that association, not its cause.

In the same design (150 replicates per scenario), for the three statistics:

nulltrait independent of nichestrait and niches on the treesorting
"species"4.0–4.7%14–23%99–100%
"phylo", \(k = 1.1\)2.7–4.0%4.0–11%95–100%
"phylo", \(k = 1.01\)1.3–4.7%2.0–10%91–100%
"bm"10–85%2.7–4.7%43–100%

The phylogenetic permutations bring the error back near the nominal level in both null scenarios, with some excess left for the correlation and the variance of \(\alpha\) when trait and niches share the tree; "bm" is exact in that scenario but fails when the trait has no phylogenetic structure, and loses power for the variance of \(\beta\).

References

Ackerly, D. D., & Cornwell, W. K. (2007). A trait-based approach to community assembly: partitioning of species trait values into within- and among-community components. Ecology Letters, 10, 135–145. doi:10.1111/j.1461-0248.2006.01006.x

Strona, G., Nappo, D., Boccacci, F., Fattorini, S., & San-Miguel-Ayanz, J. (2014). A fast and unbiased procedure to randomize ecological binary matrices with fixed row and column totals. Nature Communications, 5, 4114. doi:10.1038/ncomms5114

Lapointe, F.-J., & Garland, T., Jr. (2001). A generalized permutation model for the analysis of cross-species data. Journal of Classification, 18, 109–127. doi:10.1007/s00357-001-0007-0

Examples

set.seed(1)
tree <- treeshapesim::sim_tree_shape(20)
sim <- simulate_metacommunity(landscape_implicit(15), species_traits(tree),
                              competition_matrix(tree, "none"), n_steps = 100,
                              seed_steps = 1:5)
ind <- sample_individuals(sim, n = 5, intraspecific_sd = 1)
tg <- trait_gradient(ind, abundance = "abundance")
trait_gradient_test(tg, n_null = 99)
#> Null model of the trait-gradient analysis: 99 communities, species 
#>       statistic observed null_mean null_sd    ses    p
#>  cor_beta_alpha    0.697    -0.417    0.25  4.460 0.02
#>        var_beta   68.200    35.300   43.90  0.749 0.32
#>       var_alpha  200.000   504.000   90.60 -3.350 0.02
# the correlation of beta and alpha against the curveball
trait_gradient_test(tg, n_null = 99, null = "curveball")$statistics[1, ]
#>        statistic  observed null_mean   null_sd      ses    p
#> 1 cor_beta_alpha 0.6969889 -0.500578 0.2130449 5.621195 0.02
# means exchanged among relatives, or simulated along the tree
trait_gradient_test(tg, n_null = 99, null = "phylo", tree = tree)
#> Null model of the trait-gradient analysis: 99 communities, phylo 
#>       statistic observed null_mean null_sd    ses    p
#>  cor_beta_alpha    0.697    -0.401   0.319  3.440 0.02
#>        var_beta   68.200    41.200  41.500  0.651 0.30
#>       var_alpha  200.000   505.000  99.200 -3.080 0.02
trait_gradient_test(tg, n_null = 99, null = "bm", tree = tree)
#> Null model of the trait-gradient analysis: 99 communities, bm 
#>       statistic observed null_mean null_sd      ses    p
#>  cor_beta_alpha    0.697    -0.472   0.196  5.97000 0.02
#>        var_beta   68.200    67.800  56.600  0.00652 0.68
#>       var_alpha  200.000   878.000 452.000 -1.50000 0.02
